```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", dev.args = list(bg = "transparent"))
# Plots: transparent, with a mid-tone ink that reads on light and dark pages.
knitr::knit_hooks$set(ink = function(before, options, envir) {

    par(bg = NA, fg = "#7C7799", col = "#7C7799", col.axis = "#7C7799",

  }
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(ink = TRUE)
inline_svg <- function(file) {
  svg <- paste(readLines(file.path("figures", file), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
  knitr::asis_output(paste0("```{=html}\n", svg, "\n```\n"))
}
```

emeans fits e-means, the mini-batch alternative to k-means from Meta FAIR's
faiss library, whose authors report a lower loss than Lloyd's algorithm in
about a tenth of the epochs (Bessa et al., 2026; see `citation("emeans")`).
This vignette takes you through a first fit and then the handful of knobs you
will rarely need to touch.

## Quick start

```{r}
library(emeans)

set.seed(1)
x <- rbind(
  matrix(rnorm(6000, mean = 0, sd = 0.7), ncol = 2),
  matrix(rnorm(6000, mean = 3, sd = 0.7), ncol = 2),
  cbind(rnorm(3000, 0, 0.7), rnorm(3000, 3, 0.7))
)
fit <- emeans(x, 3, threads = 2)
fit
```

The fit is a list holding the centers, each row's cluster, the sizes and
sums of squares familiar from `kmeans()`, a per-pass `history` and the recipe
that produced it.

```{r}
fit$centers
fit$size
head(fit$history, 3)
```

`summary(fit)` prints the recipe with the tail of the history, and since
every random draw comes from R's own generator, `set.seed()` is all it takes
to make a fit reproducible.

## Plotting the clusters

Base graphics are all you need to admire the result: colour each point by
its cluster and give each center a ring so it stands out from the crowd.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of 15,000 points in three groups, coloured green, blue and amber by cluster, with a large ringed dot at the centre of each group."
cols <- c("#1F9E80", "#5F6FE0", "#C27A17")  # one colour per cluster
plot(x, col = adjustcolor(cols[fit$cluster], alpha.f = 0.45), pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
     xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2", asp = 1)
points(fit$centers, pch = 21, bg = cols, col = "white", cex = 2.4, lwd = 2.5)
points(fit$centers, pch = 1, cex = 3.1, lwd = 1.5)
```

## Comparison with `kmeans()`

`emeans(x, k)` slots into code written for `stats::kmeans(x, k)`, since the
result carries the same `cluster`, `centers`, `size`, `withinss`,
`tot.withinss`, `totss` and `betweenss` and answers to `predict()`; the one
difference worth knowing is that `iter` counts batch updates rather than
Lloyd iterations.

Three well-separated blobs flatter any method, so here is a harder test: 25
blobs on a grid, with both methods starting from the same 25 points and
allowed the same number of passes over the data. Each is scored by its error,
`tot.withinss / nrow(y)`, the mean squared distance from a point to its
nearest center.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
grid <- as.matrix(expand.grid(1:5, 1:5)) * 4
y <- grid[sample(25, 25000, replace = TRUE), ] +
  matrix(rnorm(50000, sd = 0.8), ncol = 2)
start <- y[sample.int(nrow(y), 25), ]

lloyd <- function(passes) {
  suppressWarnings(kmeans(y, start, iter.max = passes, algorithm = "Lloyd"))
}
em6 <- emeans(y, 25, centers = start, nepochs = 6, threads = 2)
```

Here is where each method stands after six passes:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of the same 25 grey blobs on a five by five grid, each with its 25 centers marked. Left, kmeans() after six passes: several blobs share two centers while others have none. Right, emeans() after six passes: every blob but two has a center of its own; one center sits between two blobs in the top row and one blob in the second row has two. Each panel's title gives its error."
fits <- list("kmeans()" = lloyd(6), "emeans()" = em6)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 0.5))
for (name in names(fits)) {
  plot(y, pch = 16, cex = 0.3, col = adjustcolor("#7C7799", alpha.f = 0.15),
       asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = sprintf("%s, error %.2f", name, fits[[name]]$tot.withinss / nrow(y)))
  points(fits[[name]]$centers, pch = 21, bg = cols[2], col = "white", cex = 1.9, lwd = 2)
}
```

Following the error pass by pass tells the same story. For `kmeans()` each
point on the line is a fresh run allowed one more Lloyd iteration than the
last, while e-means logs the error of every pass in `fit$history` as it
goes.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of error against passes over the data, from one to six, for kmeans() and emeans(). The emeans() line falls below the kmeans() line within the first passes and stays there."
passes <- 1:6
error <- rbind(
  kmeans = sapply(passes, function(p) lloyd(p)$tot.withinss / nrow(y)),
  emeans = em6$history$obj / em6$history$rows
)
matplot(passes, t(error), type = "o", lty = 1, pch = 16, lwd = 2.5,
        col = cols[c(3, 2)], xlab = "passes over the data", ylab = "error")
legend("topright", c("kmeans()", "emeans()"), col = cols[c(3, 2)],
       lwd = 2.5, pch = 16, bty = "n")
```

Six passes in, Lloyd's algorithm still has blobs sharing a center while
their neighbours go without, whereas e-means does most of its work in the
first pass and has settled by the second, although even it leaves one blob
with a center to spare.

## How the centroids move

Each batch is assigned to its nearest centroids, and every centroid then
moves part of the way toward the mean of the batch points it won. How far it
moves depends on a weight `w` that grows with the number of those points and
with the step size `alpha`, while the running count `N` behind it is an
exponential moving average, so old batches fade from memory instead of
weighing on the centroid forever.

```{r}
#| echo: false
inline_svg("update.svg")
```

The step size starts at `alpha0` and glides along a cosine to a tenth of
that by the last update. During the final pass emeans also keeps each
cluster's exact sums, so every cluster that received points in that pass
finishes at their exact mean, a closing flourish that tidies up whatever
wobble the moving averages left behind.

```{r}
#| echo: false
inline_svg("schedule.svg")
```

## The recipe

Left to its own devices, `emeans()` picks the batch size, the initial step
size `alpha0` and the revival threshold from the number of rows, `k` and the
dimension, then files the whole recipe away in the fit:

```{r}
str(fit$recipe[c("nepochs", "batch_size", "alpha0", "epoch_rows")])
```

You can override any piece with `nepochs`, `batch_size`, `alpha0`,
`batch_law` or `unused_threshold`, and `nepochs` may even be fractional,
though a budget so stingy that an epoch would hold no rows is an error.

```{r}
fit2 <- emeans(x, 3, nepochs = 2, batch_size = 256, threads = 2)
fit2$recipe$batch_size
```

## Predicting

`predict()` assigns new rows to their nearest center or, with
`type = "distance"`, returns that center's score:

```{r}
newx <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(3, 3), c(0, 3))
predict(fit, newx)
predict(fit, newx, type = "distance")
```

For the training rows `fit$cluster` gives the same answer as
`predict(fit, x)`, because `emeans()` finishes with a sweep that labels every
row by its nearest final center and adds up the sums of squares on the way.
On very large data `keep_cluster = FALSE` skips that sweep and saves roughly a
pass, at the price of the labels and sums of squares. When the fit used
`max_points_per_centroid`, the rows left out of training appear in
`fit$cluster` as `NA`, though `predict()` will label them for you.

## Spherical mode

With `spherical = TRUE`, e-means clusters unit vectors by inner product and
leaves normalising the data to you.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
angle <- c(rnorm(500, 0), rnorm(500, 2), rnorm(500, 4))
y <- cbind(cos(angle), sin(angle))
sph <- emeans(y, 3, spherical = TRUE, threads = 2)
sph$centers
rowSums(sph$centers^2)
```

In this mode `predict(type = "distance")` returns the inner-product
similarity rather than a squared distance, so bigger now means closer.

## Odds and ends

`threads` defaults to `getOption("emeans.threads", 2L)` and bows to any cap
set in the `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT` environment variable. R for macOS ships without
OpenMP, so Mac builds run serially unless you configure the compiler
otherwise.

The deliberate differences from the upstream Python implementation are listed
under "Differences from upstream" in `?emeans`.
